Now let me compile the verse-by-verse notes from what I've gathered:

# 1 Samuel 9 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview
The chapter introduces Saul, Israel's first king. The inspired compiler relates Saul's genealogy and description (vv. 1–2), his providential meeting with Samuel while searching for lost donkeys (vv. 3–14), God's prior revelation to Samuel (vv. 15–17), the meeting and feast (vv. 18–24), and the private conference on the rooftop (vv. 25–27). The whole narrative is "singularly picturesque" (Ellicott), demonstrating God's sovereign orchestration of seemingly trivial events.

---

### v. 1 — Kish, Saul's father, and his lineage
**Traditional reading:** Kish was "a mighty man of power" (KJV) — the Hebrew term *gibbor chayil* can mean a man of **wealth, standing, or valor**. The ESV and NLT translate it "a man of wealth"; NET has "a prominent person." Saul came from an affluent, influential Benjamite family. Gill notes Kish's name may mean "ensnared," though the reason is uncertain. The genealogy back to Aphiah establishes Saul's genuine Benjamite pedigree. The Pulpit Commentary notes that Benjamite genealogies are "hopelessly entangled" due to the near-extermination of the tribe in Judges 20:48; only 600 men survived at the rock Rimmon, and any ancestor of Saul must have been among them.  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-9/  
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-9-commentary  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-9.html  
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/9.htm

### v. 2 — Saul's appearance
**Traditional reading:** Saul was "choice and handsome" (*bachur*, meaning in the full flower of manhood — Pulpit). He was "head and shoulders" taller than anyone else in Israel. David Guzik remarks: "Saul looked like a great king. If being king over Israel was all about image and appearances, Saul was the man — the king from central casting." His name *Sha'ul* means "asked of God," fitting because Israel had asked for a king.  

**Key observation (multiple sources):** What is *not* mentioned in vv. 1–2 is any relationship with God. Guzik: "There is nothing said because there was nothing to say." Dale Ralph Davis (quoted at Precept Austin): "You must keep in mind this description of Saul…his ideal appearance and his physical impressiveness. File it away; it will prove important much later in our story." Bergen (NAC, cited at Precept Austin) notes that Saul is the only Israelite in Scripture whose height is specifically noted — elsewhere only Israel's *enemies* had their height mentioned (Num 13:33; Deut 1:28; 1 Sam 17:4). Israel wanted a king "like all the other nations," and God gave them one down to the physical details.  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-9/  
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-9-commentary  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-9.html

### v. 3 — The lost donkeys
**Traditional reading:** The donkeys (Hebrew: "she-asses," kept for breeding and riding — Pulpit) wandered off. Kish sent Saul with one servant to search. This seemingly trivial domestic annoyance becomes the hinge of national history. Guzik: "We have no idea how God will use the seemingly normal — and annoying — circumstances of life." Precept Austin: "There were no chance occurrences in Saul's life nor are there in ours."  

Jewish tradition (noted by Gill) held that the servant was Doeg the Edomite, though this is speculative.  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-9/  
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-9-commentary  
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/9.htm

### v. 4 — The fruitless search
**Traditional reading:** Saul passed through Mount Ephraim, Shalisha (probably the region around Baal-shalisha, "Three-land," named for three converging valleys — Pulpit), Shaalim ("jackal-land," a wild, uninhabited region — Pulpit), and the land of Benjamin — but found nothing.  

Guzik: "This was frustrating to Saul. Yet, God was working out His plan through the lost donkeys, in a way Saul couldn't even imagine." Precept Austin notes the repeated "but they did not find them" shows Saul's diligence, and that the donkeys "went where God wanted them." Spurgeon (quoted at Precept Austin): "It is important for us to learn that the smallest trifles are as much arranged by the God of providence as the most startling events. He who counts the stars has also numbered the hairs of our heads."  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-9/  
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-9-commentary  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-9.html

### v. 5 — Saul's concern for his father
**Traditional reading:** Arriving at the land of Zuph (where Ramathaim-zophim, Samuel's home, was located — Pulpit and Gill), Saul urged returning home lest Kish stop worrying about the donkeys and start worrying about them. This reveals Saul's **filial thoughtfulness** — a positive trait. James Smith (Handfuls of Purpose, quoted at Precept Austin): "He was not so anxious about the objects of his pursuit as to forget the anxious thoughts of a loving father."  
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-9-commentary  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-9.html

### v. 6 — The servant's suggestion
**Traditional reading:** The servant pointed out that in "this city" (Ramah) there was "a man of God" who was "highly respected" and whose words always came true. Guzik calls this "a great credit to Samuel" — his reputation was so strong that even men of little spiritual character thought to consult him about lost donkeys. Yet Guzik also notes the servant and Saul "weren't men of much spiritual character" — they thought of the prophet mainly as someone who might help find donkeys, not for genuine spiritual guidance. The Church Pulpit Commentary observes: "His servant knew better than he to whom to turn."  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-9/  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-9.html

### v. 7 — Saul's concern about a gift
**Traditional reading:** Saul worried they had nothing to bring the man of God — their bread was gone and they had no gift. In the ancient Near East, it was customary to approach a great man with a present (cf. 1 Ki 14:3; 2 Ki 8:8–9 — noted by Guzik/Youngblood). Guzik cautions: "It is wrong to think that Samuel had some type of fee for his 'prophetic services.' Samuel was a great prophet of the living God, not a fortune-teller." The Pulpit Commentary says the word for "present" (*teshurah*) is rare and "apparently is the technical name for a fee of this kind, half payment and half gift."  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-9/  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-9.html

### v. 8 — The quarter shekel of silver
**Traditional reading:** The servant had a quarter-shekel of silver (about sevenpence-halfpenny in Gill's 18th-century estimate). The Pulpit Commentary notes that the shekel was "roughly stamped" and "divided into four quarters by a cross, and broken when needed." The servant's willingness to part with all his money shows eagerness. Gill remarks that both Saul and his servant "must entertain a mean opinion of prophets" to think Samuel would take money for finding donkeys, though "something of this kind was done by prophets…which might be permitted to keep the people from going to diviners and soothsayers."  
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/9.htm  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-9.html

### v. 9 — The editorial gloss on "seer"
**Traditional reading:** This parenthetical note explains that "the prophet of today was formerly called the seer" (*ro'eh*). The Pulpit Commentary says this verse "is evidently a gloss, written originally by some later hand in the margin" to explain the older term. It notes that *ro'eh* refers to ordinary-sight vision, while *chozeh* refers to ecstatic vision; *ro'eh* was a popular term that became somewhat degraded over time, while *nabi* ("prophet") was the "older and established word." Some Jewish commentators (Gill notes) suggested this verse was added by Ezra or Jeremiah, but Gill argues Samuel himself could have written it, since in his youth the term "seer" was common and later "prophet" became more prevalent.  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-9.html  
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/9.htm

### vv. 10–11 — Going to the city and meeting the maidens
**Traditional reading:** Saul agreed ("Well said") and they went. As they climbed the hill to Ramah (which means "high," built on a double hill — Pulpit), they met young women drawing water and asked if the seer was there. Gill notes a Jewish tradition from Rabbi Akiba: meeting maidens coming out of a city before entering is a good omen — citing Abraham's servant, Jacob, Moses, and here Saul.  
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/9.htm  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-9.html

### vv. 12–13 — The maidens' detailed reply
**Traditional reading:** The young women gave remarkably detailed directions: the seer was just ahead; he had come to the city that day for a sacrifice at the high place; the people wouldn't eat until he blessed the sacrifice. The Pulpit Commentary observes that the rendering "as soon as…straightway" is "too forcible" — the maidens were "garrulous" but the Hebrew particles are milder. The "high place" (*bamah*) was at this time a legitimate site for worship of the true God — Samuel had built an altar at Ramah (1 Sam 7:17). The Pulpit Commentary notes these high places were "remains of the old patriarchal religion" and only later condemned because of their tendency to degenerate into nature-worship. The pious custom of blessing the sacrifice before eating is an ancestor of the Christian practice of "giving of thanks" before meals, inherited from the Jews.  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-9.html  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-9/

### v. 14 — The encounter with Samuel
**Traditional reading:** As Saul and his servant entered the city, Samuel was coming toward them on his way up to the high place. The timing was exact — "it 'just happened' that Saul and his servant came…on the same day Samuel was in town. God is guiding through these circumstances" (Guzik). The Pulpit Commentary notes that the Hebrew preposition means "within" the city, and that they met Samuel "in the very portal" (gateway).  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-9/  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-9.html

### v. 15 — God's prior revelation to Samuel
**Traditional reading:** "The LORD had revealed to Samuel" — literally, "had uncovered his ear" (cf. Ruth 4:4; 2 Sam 7:27). The Pulpit Commentary explains: "The phrase is taken from the pushing aside of the headdress in order to whisper, and therefore means that Jehovah had secretly told Samuel." This happened "the day before Saul's arrival." Guzik contrasts: "Saul had no relationship with the LORD, so God spoke to Saul through lost donkeys. But Samuel knew and loved the LORD, so God spoke to Samuel in his ear." Precept Austin: "God gives the exact time and states it is He who is sending Saul, clearly indicating the donkey 'two-step' was God's plan all along!"  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-9/  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-9.html  
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-9-commentary

### v. 16 — God's commission: anoint him leader
**Traditional reading:** God told Samuel to anoint Saul as *nagid* ("leader/commander," not the usual word for king) over Israel, with the specific purpose "he will save them from the hand of the Philistines." The Pulpit Commentary notes that this shows Saul's office was "essentially military," though the A.V.'s "captain" is too narrow — the word means "prince, chief." The Pulpit Commentary also observes that Samuel's earlier victory at Mizpah (ch. 7) had not "altogether broken" Philistine power, and these words "plainly" show Israel was again suffering from Philistine domination.  

**Key point (Guzik):** "Even though Israel rejected the LORD as their king (1 Samuel 8:7), God was still in control. He didn't step off His throne just because Israel asked Him to. He would indeed give them a king, but He sent a flawed king to a flawed Israel." God says "I have looked upon My people, because their cry has come to Me" — showing His grace and compassion despite their rejection. The Church Pulpit Commentary: "God has always to work with imperfect instruments. Because this is so, He does not therefore throw the instruments aside."  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-9/  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-9.html

### v. 17 — "Here is the man"
**Traditional reading:** When Samuel saw Saul, the LORD said, "Here is the man…he shall rule over My people." The Pulpit Commentary renders the Hebrew more literally: "Jehovah answered him" — meaning that as Samuel saw the towering stranger, he wondered silently whether this was the one, and God's word came in answer to his unspoken question. The marginal reading for "reign" is literally "restrain in" — i.e., coerce, control — suggesting Saul's rule would be strict and stern, a nuance lost in the general rendering of the A.V.  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-9.html  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-9/

### v. 18 — Saul's question at the gate
**Traditional reading:** Saul approached Samuel in the gateway and asked where the seer's house was — not recognizing that he was speaking to the very man he sought. The Church Pulpit Commentary: "The best people in the world are not known by the world. God works His will by unrecognized prophets."  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-9.html

### v. 19 — "I am the seer"
**Traditional reading:** Samuel identified himself, told Saul to go up before him to the high place and eat with him, and promised to tell him "all that is in your heart" in the morning. The Pulpit Commentary notes that Samuel addressed Saul in the singular ("Go up before me") as a mark of honor to the future king, while including the servant in the plural ("Ye shall eat"). Guzik: "Saul must have been amazed. He looked for a noted prophet, and the first man he asked…was the prophet."  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-9/  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-9.html

### v. 20 — The donkeys found; the desire of Israel
**Traditional reading:** Samuel told Saul the donkeys lost three days ago had been found — proving supernatural knowledge since Saul hadn't mentioned his errand. Then Samuel added the cryptic words: "Upon whom is all the desire of Israel, if not upon you and all your father's house?" The Pulpit Commentary translates this: "To whom belongs all that is desirable in Israel? Is it not for thee, and for thy father's house?" — a veiled hint that Saul would receive the kingdom.  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-9.html  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-9/

### v. 21 — Saul's humble objection
**Traditional reading:** Saul protested: "Am I not a Benjamite from the smallest tribe of Israel, and is not my clan the least of all the clans of Benjamin?" Guzik calls this "a genuinely humble response…even if it wasn't completely honest," since Saul's family was actually prominent (v. 1). Clarke (quoted by Guzik): "This speech of Saul is exceedingly modest; he was now becomingly humble; but who can bear elevation and prosperity?" The Pulpit Commentary notes that Benjamin had been "so crushed" (Judges 20) that its power was very small, and Saul's clan, though opulent, was "not a leading one."  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-9/  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-9.html

### v. 22 — The place of honor at the feast
**Traditional reading:** Samuel brought Saul and his servant into the hall (*lishkah*, the chamber attached to the high place — Pulpit) and seated them in the chief place among about thirty invited guests. The seating protocol in that culture was highly significant; the seat of honor was next to the host. Notably, even Saul's servant was honored — "as representing the king's officers of state" (Pulpit).  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-9/  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-9.html

### vv. 23–24 — The reserved portion
**Traditional reading:** Samuel told the cook to bring the special portion that had been set aside. The cook brought the leg (or shoulder — Hebrew *shoq*) "and what was attached to it" (the flesh and fat not burned on the altar — Pulpit). Samuel said it had been kept for Saul "for this occasion, from the time I said, 'I have invited the people.'"  

The Pulpit Commentary offers a detailed reconstruction: the Hebrew makes the **cook** the speaker, not Samuel (the name "Samuel" is not in the Hebrew text; the Syriac and Chaldee agree the cook speaks). The meaning: when Samuel received the revelation the previous day, he arranged the sacrifice, invited thirty chief citizens, and instructed the cook to reserve the portion of honor for the special guest. The cook's chatty explanation "is entirely after the manner of ancient times, and would show Saul how completely his coming had been foreseen and provided for."  

The Pulpit Commentary also speculates: if this was the *right* shoulder — normally the priest's portion (Lev 7:32) — Samuel may have given it to Saul "in token that the priesthood would be subject to the royal power," though it could simply have been the left shoulder, which laity could eat. Guzik suggests Samuel was testing Saul's character: "how we receive honor reveals who we truly are."  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-9.html  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-9/

### v. 25 — The rooftop conversation
**Traditional reading:** After descending from the high place into the city, Samuel spoke with Saul on the roof of his house. The Pulpit Commentary notes the Septuagint has a different reading: "they spread a bed for Saul upon the roof, and he lay down" — but the Syriac and Chaldee agree with the Hebrew text. The Pulpit Commentary suggests Samuel did not yet tell Saul he would be king (that came in the morning, ch. 10:1); rather, "Samuel might be anxious to impress on Saul's mind the great principles of the theocratic government, and also the nature of the remedies necessary for Israel's recovery from its present misery." Ellicott suggests the conversation covered "the sad religious and political decline of the people of God…the opposition of the heathen nations, the causes of the impotency of Israel to oppose their enemies, the necessity of a religious change in the people, and of a leader thoroughly obedient to the Lord" (citing Otto von Gerlach).  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-9.html  
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/9.htm

### v. 26 — Early morning departure
**Traditional reading:** They rose early; at dawn Samuel called to Saul on the rooftop to get ready. The Pulpit Commentary corrects the A.V.: Saul had slept on the roof, and "wearied out with his long wanderings and the excitement of the previous day, was fast asleep when Samuel came to him." The Hebrew reads: "And they rose early; for at the spring of the day Samuel called to Saul upon the house top, saying…" Then both went outside together.  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-9.html

### v. 27 — "Tell the servant to go on ahead"
**Traditional reading:** At the edge of the city, Samuel told Saul to send the servant ahead. Then: "But you stay for a while, and I will reveal to you the word of God." This dramatic moment set the stage for the private anointing in the next chapter. Gill: "that he might hear the better, and more attentively than in walking; such a posture was most fitting also for what was to be done, anointing him with oil." Ellicott: "The wonderment of Saul at the strange honour and distinction shown to him…was, no doubt, increased by this proposal." The Pulpit Commentary concludes: "by that Divine word he who had left his father's house in search of lost asses was summoned to a post which, if one of the greatest dignity, was full also of danger, and burdened with solemn responsibility."  
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/9.htm  
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/9.htm  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-9.html

---

## Denominational Distinctives

### Reformed / Presbyterian
While I could not retrieve specific Reformed commentaries on this chapter due to search limits, the emphasis on God's **sovereign orchestration** of events (lost donkeys, chance meetings, exact timing) found throughout the sources is fully consistent with Reformed theology. Guzik (Enduring Word, broadly evangelical/Calvinistic) repeatedly stresses that "God was still in control" even when Israel rejected Him. The Pulpit Commentary (1880, broadly Reformed Anglican context) emphasizes "Divinely governed events, apparently trivial" and "God's regulation of imperfect desires and dangerous aspirations."

### Baptist
Spurgeon (quoted at Precept Austin): "Saul went out to seek his father's asses, he failed in the search, but he found a crown." Also: "It is important for us to learn that the smallest trifles are as much arranged by the God of providence as the most startling events." This reflects the Baptist emphasis on God's meticulous providence in everyday life.

### Pentecostal / Charismatic
David Guzik (Enduring Word, which is used in charismatic circles) emphasizes the **supernatural knowledge** of Samuel: "Samuel proved to Saul that he was a true prophet from God. He showed Saul he knew things that he probably could not have known unless it was revealed to him supernaturally" (v. 20). The emphasis on God speaking "in the ear" to Samuel underscores the reality of personal divine communication — a point Pentecostal readers would readily affirm.

### Lutheran
The Church Pulpit Commentary's emphasis on "two lines" — the natural course of events and the supernatural word — reflects a Lutheran "two kingdoms" sensibility: "Here are two lines along which God is acting. The first is the natural course of events…The second line is supernatural…This is how God works."  

---

## Other Views

### The "seer"/"prophet" distinction (v. 9)
The Pulpit Commentary notes that *ro'eh* ("seer") became a somewhat degraded term over time, while *nabi* ("prophet") remained the more standard and honorable designation. This reflects the development of prophetic terminology in Israel's history. The editorial gloss suggests the Books of Samuel in their final form are later than Samuel's own day.

### The identity of the cook as speaker (v. 24)
The Pulpit Commentary argues that the **cook**, not Samuel, is the speaker in v. 24 — a detail obscured by the insertion of "Samuel" in the Septuagint and Vulgate (followed by the KJV and many translations). The Syriac and Chaldee agree with the Hebrew that makes the cook the speaker. This is a text-critical note of interest.

### Saul's height and "a king like the nations"
Bergen (New American Commentary, cited at Precept Austin) makes the striking observation that **Saul is the only Israelite in Scripture noted for his height** — elsewhere only Israel's *enemies* are described as tall (Num 13:33; Deut 1:28; 2:10; 9:2; 1 Sam 17:4). This suggests that God was giving Israel precisely what they asked for: "a king like all the other nations" (1 Sam 8:20), right down to the physical characteristics that made their enemies intimidating.  
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-9-commentary

### Catholic and Orthodox
I was unable to retrieve specific Catholic/Orthodox commentary pages within the search and fetch limits. However, the patristic and medieval Catholic interpretive tradition (reflected in part by Gill's awareness of Jewish traditions, Jerome's geographical notes, and Josephus's accounts) tends to read this chapter as demonstrating God's providential preparation of a leader for His people — with Saul as a type whose initial humility foreshadows but contrasts with Christ the true King.
